intro: This group sits right at the boundary between the C++ language and the physical hardware underneath it — how memory is actually laid out, when the standard promises one thread's writes are visible to another, and what happens when your logical model of "independent variables" collides with the CPU's physical cache-line granularity. This is exactly the territory HFT interviews probe hardest, because it's where correctness and performance are both on the line simultaneously.

concepts.intro: Every type has an ALIGNMENT requirement: an object of that type may only be placed at a memory address that's a multiple of its alignment (commonly, a type's alignment equals its size for primitives, up to some platform maximum). To satisfy every member's alignment requirement inside a struct, the compiler silently inserts PADDING bytes between members as needed — which means a struct's total size, and even its layout, depends on the DECLARATION ORDER of its members, not just which members it has.

examples.title: Reordering members to eliminate padding
examples.explanation: Both structs hold exactly the same three fields — the only difference is declaration order, and that alone changes the total size by 33% here. The general heuristic: declare members from LARGEST alignment requirement to smallest to minimize padding.

examples.title: Checking layout directly
examples.explanation: This is directly checkable and is a common quick warm-up interview question: "reorder this struct to make it smaller, without removing or changing any field."

pitfalls: Assuming struct size is just the sum of its members' sizes — padding means it very often isn't, and the gap can be significant for structs mixing small (char, bool) and large (int, double, pointer) members without deliberate ordering.

Forgetting that padding also matters for ARRAYS of structs — a small per-element size increase from bad ordering multiplies across every element, directly hurting cache-line utilization when scanning the array (see False Sharing for the related-but-distinct cross-thread version of this concern).
concepts.why: A common warm-up systems question at HFT firms — packing structs tightly (message formats, order-book entries) is routine, practical work, not academic trivia.

concepts.intro: False sharing is a PERFORMANCE problem, not a correctness one: two threads write to two DIFFERENT, logically-unrelated variables that happen to land on the same CPU cache line (commonly 64 bytes). Because cache-coherence protocols track ownership at the granularity of a whole cache line, every write by either thread invalidates the OTHER core's cached copy of that entire line — even though the two threads never actually touch each other's data. The threads end up fighting over cache-line ownership as if they were racing on the same variable, when logically they aren't. The fix is to pad/align each independently-hot variable to its own cache line, commonly via `alignas(64)`.

examples.title: The problem: two "independent" atomics sharing a cache line
examples.explanation: Both threads are correct (each only touches its own atomic), but performance suffers as if they were contending on a single shared variable, purely because of physical cache-line proximity.

examples.title: The fix: force each hot variable onto its own cache line
examples.explanation: `alignas(64)` forces each field to start at a 64-byte-aligned address, and the compiler pads the struct so the SECOND field can't share a line with the first — the increased memory footprint is the explicit price for removing the false-sharing bottleneck entirely.

pitfalls: Diagnosing this as a "race condition" because a profiler shows contention-like symptoms — false sharing produces performance symptoms that superficially resemble lock contention, but there's no actual shared logical state; the fix (cache-line separation) is completely different from the fix for a real race (synchronization).

Over-applying `alignas(64)` everywhere defensively — it's a real memory-footprint cost, worth paying specifically for variables that are BOTH hot (frequently written) AND touched by different threads; padding cold or single-threaded data this way is pure waste.
concepts.why: One of THE most frequently asked HFT-specific interview questions, almost always phrased exactly as: "two threads write to adjacent memory locations — what happens, and how would you fix it?"

concepts.intro: The C++11 memory model formally defines, for multithreaded programs, WHEN a write by one thread is guaranteed to be visible to a read by another thread. Absent any synchronization at all, concurrently accessing the same memory location from multiple threads — with at least one of those accesses a write — is a **data race**, which the standard defines as undefined behavior, not merely "you might read a stale value." Synchronization operations (atomics with appropriate ordering, mutexes) establish a **happens-before** relationship between specific operations in different threads, and it's ONLY through such an established happens-before edge that one thread's writes are guaranteed visible to another's subsequent reads.

examples.title: A data race: undefined behavior, not just "maybe stale"
examples.explanation: This isn't merely "probably works but might occasionally see a stale value" — it's genuine undefined behavior per the standard, because there's no happens-before relationship connecting Thread 1's writes to Thread 2's reads at all.

examples.title: The fix: establishing happens-before via release/acquire atomics
examples.explanation: The release store and the acquire load that observes it form a synchronization point: everything sequenced-before the release in Thread 1 is guaranteed visible after the acquire in Thread 2 — this release/acquire handoff pattern is the fundamental building block of essentially all lock-free code.

pitfalls: Assuming `volatile` provides thread-safety or ordering guarantees in the way atomics do — it does not; `volatile` in C++ only prevents certain compiler optimizations (relevant for memory-mapped hardware registers) and has NOTHING to do with the multithreaded memory model or cross-thread visibility.

Believing a data race just means you occasionally get a slightly wrong/stale value — the standard defines it as full undefined behavior, which in practice can also mean the compiler optimizes based on the (false) assumption that the race never happens, producing results far stranger than "stale data."

concepts.intro: `std::atomic<T>` operations are indivisible (no other thread can observe a "half-finished" read or write), and each operation can specify an ordering constraint controlling how it interacts with OTHER memory operations around it. `memory_order_relaxed` gives you ONLY atomicity — no ordering guarantee relative to anything else — useful when you genuinely just need a value to update atomically (an independent counter) with no cross-thread visibility requirement on anything else. `memory_order_acquire` (on a load) and `memory_order_release` (on a store) together form the classic handoff pattern described in the memory-model concept above. `memory_order_seq_cst` (the default if you don't specify one) is the strongest and simplest to reason about: it additionally guarantees a single, globally-agreed total order across ALL seq_cst operations from every thread — at a real, measurable synchronization cost compared to relaxed/acquire-release.

examples.title: Relaxed: atomicity without ordering, for an independent counter
examples.explanation: Using `memory_order_seq_cst` here (the default) would still be CORRECT, just needlessly expensive — relaxed is exactly sufficient because nothing else in the program depends on this counter's update being ordered relative to anything else.

examples.title: Why the ordering choice is a real, measurable engineering decision
examples.explanation: This is exactly the kind of judgment call an HFT interviewer wants to see you reason through explicitly: relaxed is cheaper, but only correct when NOTHING else depends on ordering — defaulting to relaxed everywhere "for speed" without checking that is a real bug risk, not a free win.

pitfalls: Defaulting to `memory_order_relaxed` everywhere to "go fast" without verifying that no other code depends on ordering relative to that atomic — this converts a performance optimization into a correctness bug.

Confusing `is_lock_free()` with a promise about ordering — is_lock_free() only tells you whether the atomic avoids an internal mutex on this platform; it says nothing about which memory_order semantics you've chosen or need.

concepts.term: Undefined Behavior vs Unspecified vs Implementation-defined
concepts.intro: Three distinct levels of "the standard doesn't fully pin this down," and confusing them is a common mistake. **Undefined behavior (UB)** means the standard imposes NO requirements whatsoever — literally anything is a conforming outcome, including something that looks like it "worked" on your machine today and breaks on a different compiler, optimization level, or even a later run of the same binary. **Unspecified behavior** means the standard allows multiple valid outcomes and does not require an implementation to document which one it picked (classic pre-C++17 example: the order function-call arguments are evaluated in). **Implementation-defined behavior** is unspecified behavior with one extra requirement: each implementation MUST document, consistently, which choice it makes (e.g. the exact size of `int`, or how right-shift behaves on negative signed integers pre-C++20).

examples.title: All three, side by side
examples.explanation: The key distinguishing question for each: does the standard require ANY specific behavior at all (no -> UB), and if there IS a required documented choice, is it required to be consistent per-implementation (yes -> implementation-defined) or not (unspecified)?

examples.title: Why "but it worked when I ran it" is not evidence of correctness
examples.explanation: This is exactly why recognizing UB matters practically, not just for interview trivia: a program exhibiting UB can pass every test you throw at it today and still be genuinely broken, because the compiler is entitled to assume UB never happens and optimize on that assumption — sometimes in ways that make the bug appear or worsen only under a different build configuration.

pitfalls: Treating "it produced the expected output when I ran it" as proof that a piece of UB-containing code is fine — UB's defining property is precisely that conforming behavior includes "happens to look right today."

Assuming unspecified behavior is as dangerous as UB — it isn't: unspecified behavior guarantees the program still does something well-defined-per-that-execution, it just doesn't tell you in advance WHICH well-defined thing; UB provides no such floor at all.
concepts.why: Recognizing that a piece of code's "expected" output is actually built on UB is frequently the ENTIRE point of a tricky output-prediction interview question — the best answer is often "this is undefined behavior, so asking for THE output is the wrong question."
